requirement: Perceptual-hash dedup: Hamming-distance threshold match offers the curator a confidence-scored linkage instead of creating a duplicate MediaReference

notes: Spec §32.7.2. FOUND 2026-09-25 as a spec-to-code gap: find_by_perceptual_hash took a max_distance and ignored it, so the threshold was not honoured and a result could not be read as 'these are similar'. Now an application-side Hamming search ordered closest-first: the SQL narrows to perceptual_hash IS NOT NULL and the distance is computed in Rust, because neither backend can score hex without a dialect extension. NULL, non-hex and mismatched-width hashes are skipped rather than folded into a large distance, and one malformed row cannot hide a good match. The [media_resilience] config table is wired for the first time (enabled, perceptual_hash_algorithm, perceptual_match_threshold, require_curator_confirmation_below/above, audio_fingerprint), and validate() refuses an unknown algorithm or an out-of-range threshold. Two smaller defects found and fixed alongside: perceptual_match_threshold_is_valid was dead code, and the load_from() test helper reused a directory keyed only by (pid, name), so two tests sharing a name read the first one's config - a refusal test loaded a valid file and passed. Still open in M32-07b: no importer computes a perceptual hash yet, so nothing populates the column this search reads; the config keys are read by the route only.

requirement: Compute and store a perceptual hash when media bytes are fetched, so the dedup search has something to match on
evidence: domain::media_resilience::difference_hash (dHash, 9x8 resample); app::media_fetch::{plan_fetch, classify_with_length, MediaFingerprint, content_hash}; db::media_resilience::record_fingerprint; 6 domain tests, 17 in crates/app/tests/media_fetch.rs, 5 persistence tests in crates/app/tests/media_resilience.rs
notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the gap M32-07a left: perceptual_hash was only ever written by a test, so the dedup search read an empty column. Three parts, each tested. (1) difference_hash computes a real 64-bit dHash - resample to a fixed 9x8 grid and compare each sampled pixel with the one to its left. The grid is fixed rather than derived from the input, which is the only reason hashes of two differently-sized copies of one image are comparable. My first implementation walked pixels until it had 64 bits, so a 16x16 image contributed only its first five rows and two images differing entirely below the top half hashed identically; only a test that varies the bottom of the image caught that. (2) plan_fetch is the SSRF guard on the fetch path, delegating to the existing scrapers::safety::is_forbidden_ip and is_local_hostname rather than carrying a second weaker list. It reads url.host() and matches url::Host::{Ipv4,Ipv6,Domain} - host_str().parse::<IpAddr>() returns None for every IPv6 literal because the string keeps its brackets, so the string form silently skipped [::1], [fe80::1] and [::ffff:127.0.0.1], exactly the addresses the check exists to catch; v4-mapped v6 is unwrapped with to_ipv4_mapped() on top. (3) record_fingerprint persists both hashes, refuses a missing row rather than reporting a fetch successful for a deleted reference, and stores perceptual_hash as NULL - never an empty string - when a body could not be decoded, because two empty strings are distance 0 apart and would merge every undecodable image into one reference. Two judgement calls worth recording: plain HTTP is allowed but reported as insecure rather than refused, because a mirror may simply serve images over HTTP and refusing would be a surprise; and perceptual_hash_algorithm now defaults to dhash, not phash, since dHash is the only algorithm this build computes and a default naming an unbuilt one makes a stock instance advertise a dedup it cannot perform. Spec §32.7.2's example and docs/config-reference.md were updated to match, and the enum's doc now says which variants are implemented. Image decoding was the open piece and landed in M32-07c: `image = "=0.25.6"` (pinned exactly because 0.25.7+ needs Rust 1.85 and the workspace declares rust-version 1.82), features png/jpeg/gif/webp/bmp, 14 transitive deps and no rayon. Still open: phash/whash/ahash remain unimplemented and are refused at compute time, audio_fingerprint is still unapplied to audio, and there is still no media job kind or fetch loop that drives the fetch path - the guard, the decode and the write are tested at their boundaries rather than by a queued job.

requirement: Decode fetched image bytes to pixels so a real perceptual hash is computed rather than stored NULL
evidence: app::media_fetch::fingerprint_encoded; image 0.25.6 (pinned, MSRV 1.70); MAX_DECODED_PIXELS = 80_000_000; 6 decoding tests in crates/app/tests/media_fetch.rs (23 total in the file)
notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the last gap M32-07b named: a fetched JPEG/PNG could be content-hashed exactly but not perceptually, because nothing could turn bytes into pixels. fingerprint_encoded decodes to luma and fingers both hashes in one call; anything it cannot decode returns None so the caller stores the exact hash with a NULL perceptual one rather than a guess. Two decisions worth recording. The size limit is applied to the DECODER (ImageReader::limits with max_image_width/height), not checked after decoding: load_from_memory has already allocated by the time a caller can measure the result, so a post-decode check documents intent and prevents nothing - image's own defaults leave width and height unbounded and cap only max_alloc at 512 MiB, so a sub-cap but oversized image still gets built. image::Limits is #[non_exhaustive] so it is built from Default and mutated. And the exact pin: image 0.25.7 requires Rust 1.85 and 0.25.10 requires 1.88, so an unpinned cargo add moves the workspace MSRV floor from its declared 1.82 without failing on this 1.98 toolchain; =0.25.6 declares 1.70. And the bomb fixture originally emitted width*height zero bytes, making its own test 33 seconds; it now emits one real row, which is what a bomb looks like, and runs in 0.00s. requirement: Drive the fetch end to end in the worker so a media reference's hashes are computed from a real request
evidence: domain::jobs::JobKind::MediaFetch; app::media_job::{enqueue_media_fetch, handle_media_fetch}; app::worker dispatch arm; POST /api/v1/works/{id}/media-references enqueues; 12 end-to-end tests in crates/app/tests/media_fetch_job.rs (real HTTP server, real PNGs)
notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the last structural gap in the chain. M32-07b and M32-07c built the guard, the decoder and the write, and M32-07b's handoff recorded that record_fingerprint had NO production caller -- the 'a parser is not a feature' shape. This adds JobKind::MediaFetch (the job_kinds! macro emits the enum, ALL_KINDS, as_str and parse from one source, and kind_index/resource_class are exhaustive matches, so a new kind cannot be handled everywhere except the list), the worker handler, and the enqueue call in add_media_reference -- whose existing comment promised 'content hash computed async by the pipeline'. The handler runs the whole sequence: confirm the reference exists, take the first availability link by priority, refuse the URL, resolve the host, fetch with the instance client, classify before reading the body, read bounded, fingerprint, record. A job rather than request work because the URL is author-supplied and a slow or dead mirror must not hold an author's connection open; the payload names only the reference id, so no job row carries a URL and a corrected link is picked up by a retry. Classification is honoured, not lumped: 404/410 and a non-image are Fatal, 429/5xx and a connect or read failure are Transient, and a reference with no availability link is Fatal rather than a job that retries for the life of the instance. The body is read chunk-by-chunk against MAX_MEDIA_BYTES so a server that declares no Content-Length cannot send unbounded data. The most important decision: testing this against a loopback server required touching the SSRF guard, and my first cut took a trusted_address: Option<IpAddr> and branched AROUND the guard. It failed immediately -- the literal-address rejection lives inside plan_fetch, so the branch was never reached -- and it was wrong regardless, because a bypassed guard leaves a second, untested path through the most security-sensitive function in the chain. The working shape is plan_fetch_allowing(url, allow, timeout) with plan_fetch delegating to it with an empty slice: scheme, local-name and resolution checks all still run, production has exactly one path, and the allowlist applies to both the literal-address and the DNS-resolution check so the two cannot disagree. A test also had to stop deciding transience from error text: it looked for the substring 'transient' and failed on a correct message that said 'retrying'. The assertion is now on the error TYPE, with the prose kept in the assertion message. HandlerError gained Display and Error impls so it can be formatted normally. The 201 response now carries fingerprint_job_id. Gate: clippy 0/0, fmt clean, 82 suites with 0 failures.

requirement: Roadmap consensus repository: 12 previously untested functions with 48 tests across upsert_card/find_card_by_title_normalized/list_cards/arena_candidates/create_ballot/fetch_ballot/mark_voted/apply_elo_and_counters/record_move/list_moves/insert_suggestion/update_card_stage. The module was non-functional on PostgreSQL, the production backend: four separate decode failures, each in a function the public roadmap board calls on every page view. (1) row_to_card_postgres read matches_played/times_best/times_worst as i32 while every PG branch of list_cards selects them as CAST(... AS BIGINT), so every card failed to decode. (2) list_cards read created_at/updated_at (TIMESTAMPTZ) as String in all four branches. (3) fetch_ballot read the JSONB columns card_ids and served_elo as String. (4) list_moves read moved_by (UUID) and created_at (TIMESTAMPTZ) as String. All four fixed by rendering the non-text types as text in the PG SELECTs and reading the counters as i64; the SQLite arm is unchanged. Two design gaps are documented rather than fixed: the ON CONFLICT ... WHERE guard freezes a shipped or rejected card's entire row rather than only its stage, and normalize_title deletes punctuation instead of replacing it with a space so "Dark-Mode" is a duplicate of "DarkMode" but not of "Dark Mode".

requirement: Flexible bounties repository: 4 previously untested functions with 31 tests across create_bounty_typed/contribute_to_bounty/fetch_bounty/list_flexible_bounties, behind the economy page bounty board. The contribution ledger was broken on both backends. record_contribution inserted into bounty_contributions without its id column, and the two backends disagree about what that means: PostgreSQL rejects it outright (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY is NOT NULL), so a crowdfunded bounty accumulated funded_amount with no audit row at all on the production backend; SQLite accepts it and stores id = NULL, so the ledger had rows whose primary key was NULL and therefore could not identify a contribution. The caller discarded the error with `let _ =`, so neither backend reported anything. Both arms now supply a minted id and the swallowed error is logged. Verified by reverting the fix: the ledger tests fail on both backends, and the SQLite case needed a COUNT(id) assertion because a row-exists check passes there.

requirement: Instance taste settings: 4 previously untested functions (read/write/history/rollback) with 28 tests, behind the operator taste panel on /discovery. No production defect: the module already got the hard parts right -- every PostgreSQL SELECT renders UUID and TIMESTAMPTZ as text and widens INTEGER with ::bigint, the history insert and the settings upsert run in one transaction in that order because the settings row is a singleton and the history row is the only copy of the old values, the rows are sqlx::FromRow structs so a renamed column is a compile error, and the history is ordered by replaced_version rather than changed_at because now_rfc3339() has second precision. The tests pin those properties so none of them can be quietly undone, plus the version chain, the singleton invariant, the rollback-as-write semantics, and rolling back past version 1 landing on the config values rather than a hole. Its four pre-existing unit tests only covered the private row mappers, so nothing had ever reached the database.

notes: Spec 11.5 1.3. The counter is what lets an operator answer what the posture cost. A posture that reads what it was refused is a stronger claim than a boolean that ignored it, so it owes better accounting than the boolean did. The two numbers answer OPPOSITE questions and are deliberately not folded together: robots_overrides is 'is this instance ignoring sites?' and is something an operator may have to explain to a site's owner; robots_read_and_discarded is 'is MetadataOnly throwing away the dataset?' and non-zero means the posture is working as configured. requirement: A content fetch refused by posture is refused by name, is not retried, and a per-source override may only narrow and does not outlive its import run
evidence: robots::resolve_source_override -> Err(WideningRefused); narrows_or_equals over all nine pairs in BOTH crates; robots::caution_rank + robots::narrowest as the single order; config::RunScope (expires by being dropped, no clock); imports::run_scope_for selects the run's own non-persistent grants; imports::run_policy is the only way a run builds a policy; posture_for_source_in takes narrowest(run, file); catalogue reports robots_posture + instance_robots_posture + override_of; 15 mutations (E1-E9, F1-F6) in docs/plans/crawling-retention-preservation.md, all turn the suite red
notes: COMPLETE for the local build. Run scoping is a DROP, not a timer: run() builds a RunScope, hands it to run_policy, and the value dies with the run, so 'expired' and 'the run ended' are the same event and cannot drift. A run grant is OUTRANKED, not refused - posture_for_source_in takes narrowest(run, file), so a caller granting itself permissive against a strict config still fetches strict. TWO TRAPS, both hit here. (1) The rank order: low is the MOST cautious (Strict=0) and the rule is rank(asked) <= rank(instance). Strict=0 with >= reads correctly and is exactly backwards - it lets a strict instance accept a permissive override. Asserting one pair cannot catch an inverted order, so all nine are asserted twice. (2) A second rank was written in config.rs for the narrowest-of-two rule and it ranked Permissive as 0 - the same inversion in a second place. The fix was ONE exported caution_rank in the module that owns the enum. Also: a non-serde-defaulted map on a deny_unknown_fields struct made every existing config fail to parse ('missing field robots_posture_overrides'), which a purely additive option must never do. F4 and F5 SURVIVED and the finding was NOT a missing test: run_scope_for was REDUNDANT. posture_for_source already returns a persistent:false override on every lookup, so the run's grant and the file's answer were the same posture for the same source and the scope could not change any outcome. A path that cannot change a result is dead weight, so it was deleted - run_scope_for now returns an empty RunScope, the file answers, and F4/F5 are recorded as vacuous rather than quietly dropped. RunScope survives as the channel for mid-run grants from a caller, narrowed by narrowest(run, file) so it can never widen.

requirement: The decision client speaks the model's actual wire format
evidence: crates/decisions/src/lib.rs, pinned by a_yes_no_question_is_spelled_noul_on_the_wire, the_request_carries_a_key_once_and_the_model_wants_it_once, a_request_body_is_model_state_and_questions_and_nothing_else. Verified end to end by `cargo run -p lorehaven-decisions --bin probe` on thinkcentre.
notes: Both bugs here were found ONLY by the running model, which answered 422 where curl had answered 0.9965: the question type is `noul` and not `yesno`, and the key must appear only as the object key and not repeated inside the value. A mock written from the same reading of the docs accepts both, which is why these are wire-format assertions rather than round trips. The error body is now kept on DecisionError::Status; discarding it turned a one-line diagnosis into a bisect.

requirement: The decision audit records what was decided and on what evidence, and never the text it judged
evidence: migration 0088 in both dialects, crates/db/src/decision_audit.rs, and the route at GET /api/v1/decisions/audit (was an unconditional { items: [] }). Tests: a_null_posterior_survives_the_round_trip_as_null_and_not_as_zero, the_row_where_the_model_narrowed_keeps_both_answers, a_second_decision_about_one_subject_adds_a_row_rather_than_replacing_one, the_trail_carries_the_subject_id_and_never_the_graded_text, has_a_model_narrowed_anything. 12 mutations killed.
notes: Three decisions, each load-bearing. The subject is an id and never the graded text: an audit holding the words it judged would be a second copy of a reader's writing with none of the first copy's rules -- no deletion path, no export, no visibility level, no author who can see it. Both answers are stored, because the rows that PROVE the model stayed one-directional are exactly those where deterministic != outcome. A NULL posterior is not zero confidence: four situations produce it and collapsing them into 0.0 tells an operator a model confidently said no. has_a_model_narrowed_anything asks the safety property of the RECORDED ROWS rather than asserting it in a test, and deliberately has no query for the converse, so the property that must never hold has no code path that could claim it does.

requirement: The instance discloses which provider classifies, to every reader, and nothing about where it runs
evidence: DecisionsSummary in crates/app/src/routes/meta.rs. Tests: an_instance_that_configured_nothing_still_discloses_a_provider, a_calibrated_instance_says_so_to_a_reader_who_is_not_signed_in, the_disclosure_names_the_provider_and_nothing_about_where_it_runs, the_retention_disclosure_beside_it_is_untouched. 5 mutations killed, including always-says-deterministic, a hardcoded threshold, and leaking base_url or api_key.
notes: Amendment 3.4, beside the retention disclosure body_audience_indistinguishability.rs already pins. A DETERMINISTIC instance reports "deterministic" rather than omitting the field: a missing field is indistinguishable from an old server, and a client that renders it as "the instance does not filter" has been told something false. Exactly three fields -- provider, accept_threshold, consult_floor -- and the test pins the key SET, so a fourth field cannot slip past. The no-leak test is scoped to the decisions block rather than the whole body, because /meta already carries a correct top-level base_url and a whole-body scan for "base_url" fails against it.

requirement: The composer shows a live confidence percentage that a draft would be flagged as passive-aggressive or hostile
evidence: docs/spec-amendments/composer-positivity-indicator.md. Measured against the live model on thinkcentre, not from vendor docs.
notes: REJECTED ON MEASUREMENT. 28 labelled texts (10 hostile, 18 clean, 8 of them hard negatives -- sharp but legitimate criticism). No threshold works: at 0.5 it catches 3/10 hostile while false-flagging 0/18 clean. The misses are the interesting cases: 'I bet your mother would be ashamed of you' scores 0.075, 'your reading comprehension is genuinely shocking' 0.010, BELOW the worst clean text (0.0425). Not a prompt problem: 5 further framings (insult, belittling, passive-aggressive, dismissive, attacking-a-person) gave 0/30 combinations reaching 0.5. Latency p50 2.6-2.8s, p95 3.3s against the vendor's 'well under a second', so 'every 500ms' is off by 5x and a live indicator would be visibly stale behind the writer. The model detects OVERT insult and profanity, not indirect or demeaning hostility. The lesson: a calibrated probability is calibrated to the QUESTION IT WAS ASKED -- Laya's noul is well-calibrated for 'contains profanity or an overt insult', and reading it as an answer about passive aggression is the error the familiar 0-1 format makes easy. Rejected partly on policy: the clean texts scoring highest are exactly the honest criticism a forum exists for, so any threshold low enough to catch the misses starts punishing them, and that is the operator's call.

requirement: A column added to a PII-bearing table cannot be published until the snapshot policy classifies it
evidence: scripts/check-snapshot-pii.py (exit 0, 2014 columns / 276 tables) + --self-test (exit 0, 4 properties). Found RED on 4 undecided columns on first run, 2 of them added by M59-10 hours earlier. Gate gained a CONTENT_NAME_RE fan-out after it proved silent on reader_body_copies.plain_text; the fan-out then surfaced 5 more ungated body columns, all decided. 4th self-test probe added so the fan-out cannot be deleted unnoticed.
notes: The inventory is DERIVED from migrations/postgres/*.sql, not hand-listed, and that is the whole design. A hand-kept list cannot detect the case it exists for: a new column is missing from BOTH the known-columns list and the policy list, so the gate passes. 1950 columns across 269 tables, 175 needing a decision. Covered tables need EVERY column decided; any other table needs one only when the name says it carries an identity. The self-test caught two real defects in the gate itself: an ^-anchored regex missed submitter_ip (real names are qualified in front -- recovery_email, user_agent, author_ip), and .match() with an unanchored pattern silently never matched. Fixing those found 12 more columns, including dmca_takedowns.claimant_email -- a natural person's email on a table no list of 'obvious' PII tables would contain, because a DMCA claimant is not a pseud. A pass means a decision EXISTS, not that it is right; the gate cannot see whether anyone thought about it, which is why each entry carries reviewed_by. Deliberately NOT committed: a generator script, because re-running it to absorb a new migration removes the human decision and the gate would always pass.

requirement: The snapshot re-key preserves the pseud_id join: one original yields one replacement, and the join survives
evidence: migrations/postgres/0092_snapshot_rekey.sql (snapshot_pseud, snapshot_account) + crates/app/tests/snapshot_rekey.rs
notes: Six properties, each with the failure it catches, verified against a real Postgres. 6 mutations killed. A per-row re-key passes 'does it run' and restores cleanly; the result is a set of unrelated tables and a dataset with no value, and nothing complains until someone uses it. The two functions are separate BY DESIGN: sharing a salt means anyone holding a re-keyed pseud_id table can join it to the re-keyed accounts table and recover exactly the mapping the snapshot withholds -- a failure invisible to any test that checks one function at a time, and the reason 11.16.3b calls account_id the key a first draft misses. A finding that changed the pipeline design: the re-key CANNOT be applied in place in any order. Updating the child first trips works_owner_pseud_id_fkey (parent does not hold the new value yet); updating the parent first trips it too (child still holds the old one). The constraint is per-statement, so no ordering of two statements satisfies both. The pipeline must copy to a scratch database and mask there. Found by running it, not by reading the spec. Also: CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto is in the migration, because it applied cleanly against a long-lived database where it had been installed by hand and then failed on a fresh scratch database -- a migration that only works on the database its author tested against fails on every operator's clean install.

requirement: The snapshot re-key produces a version-4 UUID, not merely a string that parses as one
evidence: crates/app/tests/snapshot_rekey.rs::the_rekey_is_a_version_four_uuid_and_not_merely_a_uuid_shaped_string
notes: Characters 15 and 20 asserted SEPARATELY from the determinism and distinctness tests, because a derivation emitting a valid-looking UUID of the wrong version passes all of those: the ::uuid cast succeeds, determinism holds, distinctness holds, and only a reader keying on the version or variant notices. Version nibble forced to 4, RFC 4122 variant nibble to a, written directly into the hash output rather than hoped for. The identity case is asserted too, and it is the one worth having: mutation-proven. Making snapshot_pseud return its input unchanged is idempotent (so determinism passes), preserves distinctness, and leaves every join intact (so the join test passes) -- 4 of the 6 tests green against a function that publishes the REAL pseud_id of a real person. the_rekey_is_not_the_identity_on_the_input exists because that mutant was found and initially survived: the first attempt at it removed only the salt, which is a weaker hash rather than the identity, and correctly still passed. The test had to target the genuine no-op to be worth anything.

requirement: doctor --strict makes a warning exit non-zero; the flag is currently declared, accepted and ignored
evidence: Verified by RUNNING the built binary, not by reading the source: on an instance with 0 failing and 1 warning, `doctor` exits 0 and `doctor --strict` exits 1 (same 19-check report both times). crates/app/src/lib.rs:139 reads args.strict; doctor::run binds _args because --strict changes the EXIT CODE and not the report, so the report is byte-identical either way.
notes: Spec 38.7.1. THE PREVIOUS NOTE WAS WRONG and is corrected here: it claimed 'doctor::run binds it as _args at doctor.rs:88 and never reads it, so --strict returns zero with 0 failing, N warnings' as a VERIFIED DEFECT. That is not a defect -- the binding in doctor::run is unused because --strict acts at the call site in lib.rs, not on the report. Correcting a row that names a source line is exactly the kind of drift docs/goal.md's correction rule exists to stop, so the claim was settled by running the binary rather than by re-reading the code.

requirement: A doctor check that could not run reports Skipped with a mandatory reason, never as ok and never bare
evidence: crates/app/src/doctor.rs tests (6 new: a skip renders as neither ok nor warn; a skip is neither a warning nor a failure; a skip carries its reason; a skip alongside a warning leaves the warning countable; plus two below). Severity gained a Skipped variant. Injections: suppressing the NOT CHECKED block fails 2, rendering a skip as 'warn' fails 2.
notes: Spec 38.7.2. VERIFIED: previously true. Severity::{Ok,Warning,Fatal} had no skip state. A Skipped variant is NOT a Warning on purpose -- a warning says 'I looked and this is wrong', a skip says 'I did not look', and if skips counted as warnings then every --strict run on a healthy instance would exit 1 over four permanent structural skips and operators would learn to ignore the exit code.

requirement: doctor's report ends with a NOT CHECKED block naming the areas it could not observe from the box
evidence: crates/app/src/doctor.rs tests: the_not_checked_block_comes_last (asserts the summary precedes it and nothing renders after), the_not_checked_block_appears_even_when_nothing_is_wrong (asserts the block prints on Report::default()), every_run_ends_by_naming_what_it_cannot_observe (pins the four structural areas). Verified by RUNNING the binary: a real doctor run prints '4 not checked' and ends with the NOT CHECKED block.
notes: Spec 38.7.3. VERIFIED: previously true -- render() ended with a count and stated nothing about coverage. Four areas are now named on EVERY run: backup restore, worker network egress, TLS termination, search index freshness. The block prints even when the list is empty, with a line saying so, because an empty block would itself read as full coverage. That last part is asserted: suppressing the block fails the test.

requirement: Every doctor check reporting Ok executed its probe; the snapshot check restores rather than reading a manifest
evidence: crates/app/src/doctor.rs tests (3 new: the_snapshot_gate_check_ran_the_script, a_gate_that_cannot_run_is_a_skip_carrying_its_reason, a_gate_that_refuses_is_reported_as_a_failure). The check spawns python3 scripts/check-snapshot-pii.py and reports the script's own last line; verified by running the binary ('24 check(s)' including snapshot-gate, 'OK: 2024 columns across 277 tables').
notes: Spec 38.7.5. Trap 3's shape was reproduced as an injection and caught -- but ONLY after the first assertion was hardened. The first version asserted the detail contained 'columns across', and an injection that hardcoded that same sentence PASSED it: Trap 3 surviving the test written for Trap 3. The assertion now runs the script and compares against its actual last line, so a hardcoded detail cannot satisfy it. Worth remembering: a test asserting on output that reporting code itself formats can be faked by the reporting code.
